title: Tunguska: The Forest Fell. Where Is the Crater? | Curio Files
description:
About 2,000 square kilometers of forest fell, yet trunks near the blast center stayed upright. No generally accepted main impact crater has been found at Tunguska. The forest left behind points instead to the sky.
Curio Files H03: follow Kulik into Siberia, from an expedition 19 years later to an old stump at the bottom of a marsh pit. See how a fast-moving body can break up in the air and send a shock wave to the ground.
Who counted 80 million trees? Why do different models give different energies? Can Lake Cheko count as an impact crater? Separate field observations, assumptions behind estimates and candidate physical evidence to see which answers hold up and which details remain unresolved.

Information current through 2026-10-12. Narration is AI-generated. AI-generated scenes reconstruct historical and scientific concepts; they are not photographs taken at the scene in 1908. Airburst diagrams are not to scale. Energy and altitude figures are research-model estimates; 80 million trees is a widely repeated rough estimate. Lake Cheko's origin and the identification of fragments remain disputed.

chapters.cheko-name: Can Lake Cheko Close the Case?

3wt8.text: Tunguska's forest fell; some central trees still stood.

m93v.text: You'd expect a huge crater at the heart of such a blast.

vu7c.text: In fact, an explosion in the air better explains this forest.

nys5.text: How could something in the sky knock trees down below?

huyj.text: A bright flash lit Tunguska, followed by a loud boom.

yy5f.text: Locals felt heat; some were knocked to the ground.

hy4f.text: Forest dwellers also recalled their tents shaking.

xs6g.text: Fallen forest covered about 2,000 square kilometers.

saq5.text: Trunks mostly fell outward, leaving a radial pattern.

pbf7.text: Local newspapers soon reported this strange event.

hyd4.text: News traveled out; reaching the site was much harder.

6qay.text: Geologist Kulik set out on a survey in 1921.

wkui.text: He failed to reach it then, only arriving in 1927.

uqmj.text: By then, 19 years had passed since the blast.

myc5.text: The team took supplies over rivers and tough bogs.

6w54.text: Wet, soft ground prolonged the search for a landing site.

zrku.text: Locals knew; the press had reported it.

xgep.text: Researchers only reached the fallen forest much later.

3np7.text: Kulik first believed an iron meteorite lay beneath the forest.

cvt5.text: A large body hitting the ground should leave a crater and debris.

j96k.text: He followed the fallen trees' direction toward the center.

fxdt.text: Time had erased many traces, but fallen trees remained.

j9da.text: He had finally arrived. Where was that meteorite hiding?

nn83.text: Outer trees lay flat, but the center was different.

c5u4.text: Some trunks stood upright, but branches and bark were damaged.

6afz.text: Outer trees fell outward, tracing the force.

8cii.text: Some central trees still stood as bare trunks.

vw49.text: The bare trunks looked like rows of utility poles.

bikj.text: Kulik still sought a crater to prove a huge meteorite lay below.

c48q.text: He turned his search to round hollows in the marsh.

2pwk.text: Researchers drained one pit to see if iron lay beneath.

44d4.text: What emerged, surprisingly, was an old tree stump.

qvf5.text: The pit gave him no hoped-for meteorite.

vf7r.text: One wrong dig could not rule out every landing site.

f2mk.text: In the following years, Kulik returned repeatedly to seek iron debris.

2uat.text: Photos and surveys from the search let later scholars reexamine the forest.

yt7z.text: Later hunts also found no accepted main impact crater.

68q7.text: No expected finds? Check the original assumptions too.

qivj.text: Was the assumed blast site wrong from the start?

f6zq.text: Trunks record the forces applied, not images of the space rock.

msxv.text: What struck the ground first may have been a blast of air.

j3mj.text: Put the blast in the sky, and the central upright trees become a clue.

54sv.text: How does an airburst's shock wave reach the ground?

derk.text: A fast body enters the air; air ahead can't move aside in time.

ih6d.text: Air is compressed fiercely, raising pressure on the body.

fdqr.text: In denser air, the body may face even greater pressure.

vfvs.text: When pressure exceeds its strength, the rock starts to break apart.

asif.text: Breakup exposes more surface to the air.

jm4w.text: Pieces slow sharply, giving kinetic energy to nearby air.

uew5.text: Rushing into air, it strongly compresses air ahead.

jm2y.text: Rock breaks, slows, and gives energy to air fast.

6s9v.text: The shock wave hits the ground, damaging the forest.

fh3w.text: It is no bomb: a space rock breaks up in the atmosphere.

8x3s.text: Below the blast center, force comes mainly from above.

za3v.text: Branches may be stripped off while trunks remain upright.

fyt5.text: Near ground zero, force hits trunks mainly from above.

hbj5.text: Farther out, greater side force fells trees outward.

a7yq.text: One airburst can leave both standing and fallen trees.

k8ac.text: Real forests have slopes and varied trees: no perfect symmetry.

musr.text: The fallen area resembles a butterfly, not a neat circle.

ew6f.text: Scientists infer the body's properties from this damage.

rz3q.text: But the rock's looseness and speed change when it breaks apart.

x7bs.text: Loose rock may break up earlier; a stronger body may hold together longer.

e4kb.text: How far fragments spread along the path changes where energy is released.

gb8q.text: A different entry angle changes where the energy goes.

r359.text: A lower estimate equals 3 to 5 million tons of TNT.

wfff.text: Another gives 10 to 30 million tons, using different assumptions.

kcfm.text: TNT equivalent compares energy. It does not mean a nuclear blast.

7uyu.text: Same energy, different height: ground damage changes.

tfp3.text: A higher blast lets the shock spread more before reaching the ground.

pefz.text: Using only the fallen area to infer the body's size leaves out key conditions.

7wqj.text: A sound airburst theory does not settle every parameter.

cti2.text: A 2019 model set puts the main blast aloft.

q8h7.text: About 10 to 14 kilometers up: an answer the model infers.

2etw.text: Older studies gave other heights, not direct readings of one event.

69ir.text: In 2013, Chelyabinsk gave us a modern comparison.

t3f2.text: A fireball crossed the daytime sky, trailing a long wake.

dcje.text: The flash was seen first; sound waves took longer to reach the ground.

k386.text: It broke up high above, yet shock waves hit the ground.

35as.text: Videos, sensor data and fallen fragments can now be cross-checked.

wxdt.text: Modern data can be checked against fragments.

34vg.text: Tunguska mostly relies on traces; we can't copy that answer.

52jj.text: How was that familiar figure of 80 million trees calculated?

vabr.text: 80 million appears in many accounts of Tunguska.

jbd7.text: It sounds precise, but nobody counted every tree from a list.

6cjz.text: A research commentary traces it to an estimate from 1933.

rkmd.text: To estimate blast energy, they first assumed a fallen area.

bb4w.text: Later maps show only about 2,000 square km of fallen forest.

8yu4.text: Assumed area: about 4 times the later mapped area.

5cus.text: Add tree density to turn that into an estimated tree count.

h5rn.text: The count assumed an area and a density of trees.

phjq.text: As citations repeated, initial assumptions slowly faded.

mkxr.text: Only 80 million remained, as though every tree had been counted.

undx.text: Dividing 80 million by 4 cannot give a new correct count.

76tt.text: We still need data on tree density, species and damage.

w2u4.text: Later surveys back about 2,000 square km.

5w6w.text: Tree counts and casualties lack equally complete data.

qvai.text: Remote does not mean empty; residents recounted the heat and damage.

8dmz.text: Death counts differ; we cannot simply claim no casualties.

e4ma.text: Did its fragments remain on the ground?

hh9k.text: If fragments fell, could a nearby lake offer a clue?

g4cw.text: The lake often mentioned is called Lake Cheko.

dd4q.text: A research team thinks a fragment may have made the lake.

6ru7.text: They studied the basin's shape and its bottom sediments.

i48k.text: But lake shape is only part of it.

huin.text: We must also ask when it formed, and what lies beneath.

gnpc.text: Sediment layers form a record we can use to estimate ages.

r9ig.text: One team thinks the lake's sediments predate 1908.

ze2w.text: If the lake already existed, that impact could hardly form it.

cjcr.text: Impact advocates later proposed a different reading.

vvez.text: Do the mud-dating methods support that age? This is disputed.

vpzm.text: Both sides also read the sediment layers differently.

addm.text: Can only an impact explain the lake's shape?

8a76.text: Did this lake really form in 1908?

znur.text: Even a rock dug up needs a proven link to that space body.

i6te.text: Deeper drilling may show what's below the lake's center.

5ig5.text: Tiny grains were found, but links to this blast are uncertain.

dqeb.text: An ordinary stone in the mud may have been there before the blast.

fbje.text: A link to 1908 needs checks on where it was found and what it is made of.

e5xj.text: Some models say fragments can survive to the ground in certain conditions.

hdg9.text: Predicted landings are far from finding a real meteorite.

43pz.text: Finding none does not prove every piece turned to gas.

9zvs.text: A rock needs a testable origin before it could help close the case.

zxin.text: So, before that last rock is found, how much can we be sure of?

3wh5.text: The blast was aloft; evidence stayed in the forest.

3umw.text: Satellites now see forest; evidence must reconstruct the details of that day.

7tip.text: Fall directions and central trunks support an airburst.

4tzv.text: Best fit: midair breakup releases energy.

uhkz.text: Most favor a stony asteroid, but its makeup and energy remain unsettled.

uu24.text: A comet fragment was a candidate, with conditions unlike a stony asteroid.

ap9b.text: An accepted physical sample is still missing to identify the body.

c4kc.text: Finding no main crater adds no weight to unsupported claims.

mvq7.text: The odd upright trees help us place the explosion back in the sky.

bavy.text: This case has open details; that does not mean we know nothing.
